Reuse. This is the accepted declaration Submission.chart_tangentSpace_eq_range_fderiv of DAG node root.minimizing_implies_stationary-a1.chart_tangent_space-a1, which is already this node's resolved prerequisite. Its frozen Lean type is byte-identical, so no new formalization is needed. It is listed so that the sibling chart_gram_factor can depend on it, matching step 2 of the selected parent proof ("By chart_tangent_space, Q(ψ(v)) = T_{ψ(v)}N = range Dψ(v)"). Its accepted natural proof follows. Only the opening Source line was adapted to this decomposition; steps 1–6 are verbatim.
Source: Simon Ch. 2 §4, (4.1)–(4.3) (book/chapter-02.txt lines 849–870). These lines give the definition of T_yM for an embedded submanifold and its identification with Dψ(ℝ^d).
1. Setup. Put y := ψ(v) ∈ W ∩ N and L := Dψ(v) = fderiv ℝ ψ v; since V is open and r ≥ 1, ψ is differentiable at v with derivative L. L is injective, so (finite dimension) there is c > 0 with |Lh| ≥ c|h| for all h ∈ ℝ^d; range L is a linear subspace, hence closed.
2. range L ⊆ T_yN. Let w = La. If a = 0, the constant curve γ ≡ y works (y ∈ N). Otherwise choose ρ > 0 with closedBall(v, ρ) ⊆ V and κ > 0 with κ|a| < ρ, and let σ(s) := κ·tanh(s/κ), a smooth function with σ(0) = 0, σ'(0) = 1 and |σ(s)| < κ. Put γ(s) := ψ(v + σ(s)a). Then v + σ(s)a ∈ V for all s, so γ is C^r (in particular C¹) on ℝ ⊇ (−1,1), γ(ℝ) ⊆ ψ(V) ⊆ N, γ(0) = y, and γ'(0) = Dψ(v)(σ'(0)a) = La = w. Hence w ∈ T_yN.
3. Embedding property. If z_k ∈ V and ψ(z_k) → y then z_k → v: the set K := {ψ(z_k) : k} ∪ {y} is compact and contained in W, so V ∩ ψ^{-1}(K) is compact and contains every z_k; any cluster point z ∈ V of (z_k) satisfies ψ(z) = y = ψ(v) by continuity, so z = v by injectivity on V; hence z_k → v.
4. T_yN ⊆ range L. Let w ∈ T_yN, witnessed by γ. As γ is continuous at 0 and W is open, there is s_0 ∈ (0,1) with γ(s) ∈ W ∩ N = ψ(V) for |s| < s_0; write γ(s) = ψ(β(s)) with β(s) ∈ V (unique by injectivity). By step 3 (applied along sequences s_k → 0), β(s) → v as s → 0.
5. Write ψ(z) − y = L(z − v) + ρ(z) with |ρ(z)| ≤ η(|z − v|)·|z − v|, η(t) → 0 as t → 0. For |s| small, η(|β(s) − v|) ≤ c/2, hence |γ(s) − y| ≥ c|β(s) − v| − (c/2)|β(s) − v|, i.e. |β(s) − v| ≤ (2/c)|γ(s) − y|. Since γ is differentiable at 0, |γ(s) − y| ≤ C|s| for small |s|; thus |β(s) − v| = O(|s|) and |ρ(β(s))| = o(|s|).
6. Hence (γ(s) − y)/s = L((β(s) − v)/s) + o(1), so the difference quotients lie within o(1) of range L. Letting s → 0, w = γ'(0) belongs to the closure of range L, which is range L. Together with step 2, tangentSpace N (ψ v) = Set.range (fderiv ℝ ψ v).
proof_key_steps: Curves s ↦ ψ(v + σ(s)a) with σ smooth, bounded, σ'(0) = 1 show range Dψ(v) ⊆ T_{ψ(v)}N.
Properness and injectivity make ψ^{-1} continuous at ψ(v) along N ∩ W.
Injectivity of Dψ(v) gives |β(s) − v| = O(|γ(s) − ψ(v)|), so difference quotients of any curve in N lie in range Dψ(v) up to o(1).

subproblems.natural_proof:
Reuse. This is the accepted declaration Submission.dsmc_chart_inverse_continuity of DAG node root.density_one_implies_regular-a1.mean_curvature_monotonicity-a1.chart_tangent_space-a1.inverse_continuity-a1. Its frozen Lean type is byte-identical, so no new formalization is needed. Its accepted natural proof follows. One sentence of the Source paragraph was adapted to say where it is used here; steps 1–8 are verbatim.
Source: Simon Ch. 2, §4, Definition (4.1) and the remark before (4.2) (book/chapter-02.txt, lines 849–862). There Simon notes that "the above definition ensures the local representation is a homeomorphism of V onto the image M ∩ W"; the properness condition of (4.1) is what makes this work. Here it supplies step 3 of the selected parent proof ("ψ is a homeomorphism onto W₀ ∩ N"; SimonGMT IsSimonLocalRepresentation.isEmbedding_chartMap) to the sibling jacobian_continuous. It is restricted to the hypotheses that step actually uses. Openness of V and W is not needed. Distances are Euclidean.
Fix v ∈ V and ε > 0, and write q := ψ(v).
1. Suppose, for a contradiction, that no δ > 0 has the stated property. Then for every j ∈ ℕ the number δ = 1/(j+1) > 0 fails. So there is v_j ∈ V with |ψ(v_j) − q| < 1/(j+1) and |v_j − v| ≥ ε.
2. We have 0 ≤ |ψ(v_j) − q| < 1/(j+1) and 1/(j+1) → 0. By squeezing, ψ(v_j) → q as j → ∞.
3. Let K := {q} ∪ {ψ(v_j) : j ∈ ℕ}. K is compact because it is the range of a convergent sequence together with its limit. Indeed, given an open cover of K, one member contains q, and by step 2 it contains ψ(v_j) for all j ≥ j₀. Finitely many further members cover ψ(v_0), …, ψ(v_{j₀−1}).
4. K ⊆ W. For each j, v_j ∈ V, so ψ(v_j) ∈ ψ(V) ⊆ W. Also v ∈ V, so q = ψ(v) ∈ ψ(V) ⊆ W.
5. By the properness hypothesis applied to the compact set K ⊆ W, the set C := V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) is compact. Every v_j lies in C, because v_j ∈ V and ψ(v_j) ∈ K. C is a compact subset of the metric space ℝ^d, hence sequentially compact. So there are a strictly increasing φ : ℕ → ℕ and a point v* ∈ C with v_{φ(i)} → v* as i → ∞. In particular v* ∈ V.
6. Now v* ∈ V, every v_{φ(i)} lies in V, and v_{φ(i)} → v*. Since ψ is continuous on V, it is continuous at v* relative to V, so ψ(v_{φ(i)}) → ψ(v*). On the other hand, (ψ(v_{φ(i)}))_i is a subsequence of (ψ(v_j))_j, so ψ(v_{φ(i)}) → q by step 2. Limits in ℝ^P are unique, hence ψ(v*) = q = ψ(v).
7. Both v* and v lie in V, and ψ is injective on V, so v* = v. Thus v_{φ(i)} → v. Hence |v_{φ(i)} − v| < ε for some i. This contradicts step 1, which gives |v_j − v| ≥ ε for every j, in particular for j = φ(i).
8. So the assumption in step 1 is false. There is δ > 0 such that every v' ∈ V with |ψ(v') − ψ(v)| < δ satisfies |v' − v| < ε. Since v ∈ V and ε > 0 were arbitrary, the statement is proved.
proof_key_steps: Negating the claim gives v_j ∈ V with |ψ(v_j) − ψ(v)| < 1/(j+1) and |v_j − v| ≥ ε, so ψ(v_j) → ψ(v).
K = {ψ(v)} ∪ {ψ(v_j)} is compact and lies in W, so V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) is compact and contains every v_j.
A subsequence v_{φ(i)} converges to some v* ∈ V. Continuity of ψ on V and uniqueness of limits give ψ(v*) = ψ(v).
Injectivity on V gives v* = v, which contradicts |v_{φ(i)} − v| ≥ ε.

Source. Steps 5, 6 and 8 of the parent proof: the Lusin–Souslin theorem, a countable chart cover via Lindelöf, disjointification, and countable additivity. Here the additivity is applied to set integrals rather than to measures. No sibling is used.

Proof. Fix a Borel set B ⊆ N and g : ℝ^P → [0, ∞].
1. (Φ maps Borel sets to Borel sets.) ℝ^P is a Polish space, and Φ is continuous and injective. By the Lusin–Souslin theorem Φ is a measurable embedding (Continuous.measurableEmbedding). So Φ(E) is Borel for every Borel E (MeasurableEmbedding.measurableSet_image).
2. (Trivial case.) If N = ∅, then B = ∅ and Φ(B) = ∅, so both sides are integrals over the empty set and equal 0. From now on assume N ≠ ∅.
3. (Countable subcover.) For each y ∈ N choose an open W_y ∋ y as in the hypothesis. The sets W_y (y ∈ N) are open and cover N. ℝ^P is second countable, hence hereditarily Lindelöf, so N is a Lindelöf set (HereditarilyLindelofSpace.isLindelof). Since N is nonempty, there is a sequence (y_k)_{k∈ℕ} in N with N ⊆ ⋃_k W_{y_k} (IsLindelof.indexed_countable_subcover).
4. (Disjoint Borel pieces.) Let S_k := B ∩ W_{y_k} and B_k := S_k ∖ ⋃_{i<k} S_i, i.e. disjointed S.
- Each S_k is Borel (B is Borel and W_{y_k} is open), hence each B_k is Borel (MeasurableSet.disjointed).
- The B_k are pairwise disjoint (disjoint_disjointed).
- ⋃_k B_k = ⋃_k S_k = B ∩ ⋃_k W_{y_k} = B, because B ⊆ N ⊆ ⋃_k W_{y_k} (iUnion_disjointed).
- B_k ⊆ S_k ⊆ W_{y_k} ∩ N, because B ⊆ N.
5. (Images.) Each Φ(B_k) is Borel by step 1. The Φ(B_k) are pairwise disjoint because Φ is injective. ⋃_k Φ(B_k) = Φ(⋃_k B_k) = Φ(B).
6. (Countable additivity.) Let E_k be pairwise disjoint Borel sets and f : ℝ^P → [0, ∞], measurable or not. Then ∫⁻_{⋃_k E_k} f dμ = Σ_k ∫⁻_{E_k} f dμ (lintegral_iUnion), because μ restricted to the union is the sum of the restrictions. Hence:
 ∫⁻_{Φ(B)} g dμ = Σ_k ∫⁻_{Φ(B_k)} g dμ, by steps 5 and 6;
 = Σ_k ∫⁻_{B_k} w(x)·g(Φ(x)) dμ(x), by the hypothesis for y_k applied to the Borel set B_k ⊆ W_{y_k} ∩ N (step 4);
 = ∫⁻_{⋃_k B_k} w(x)·g(Φ(x)) dμ(x) = ∫⁻_B w(x)·g(Φ(x)) dμ(x), by steps 4 and 6. ∎

Source. Simon Ch. 2, (4.1)–(4.2) (book/chapter-02.txt lines 849–863): a local representation is a homeomorphism of V onto W ∩ M. Also 4.11–4.12 (lines 958–981). This child is steps 3–4 of the parent proof and is exactly its first conjunct. It uses the siblings chart_gram_factor (Submission.codim1_ac_saf_chart_gram_factor) and chart_inverse_continuity (Submission.dsmc_chart_inverse_continuity).

Notation. For a linear map T : ℝ^m → ℝ^P put γ(T) := √det(⟨Te_k, Te_l⟩)_{k,l<m}, with e_k = EuclideanSpace.single k 1. J is the function of the statement.

Proof.
1. (A chart at y.) Fix y ∈ N. We show that J is continuous at y relative to N. By IsEmbeddedSubmanifold 1 m N there are an open V ⊆ ℝ^m, an open W ⊆ ℝ^P with y ∈ W, and ψ : ℝ^m → ℝ^P with: ψ is C¹ on V and injective on V; ψ(V) = W ∩ N; V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) is compact for every compact K ⊆ W; Dψ(z) is injective for z ∈ V. Since y ∈ W ∩ N = ψ(V), y = ψ(v₀) for some v₀ ∈ V.
2. (γ is continuous.) Fix k and l. The map T ↦ ⟨Te_k, Te_l⟩ is continuous on the normed space of continuous linear maps ℝ^m → ℝ^P: evaluation at a fixed vector is continuous and linear in T, and the inner product is continuous. The determinant is a polynomial in the matrix entries, hence continuous (Continuous.matrix_det), and √ is continuous. So γ is continuous.
3. (Continuous derivatives on V.) ψ is C¹ on the open set V. Φ∘ψ is C¹ on V because Φ is C¹ (ContDiff.comp_contDiffOn). The derivative of a map that is C¹ on an open set is continuous there (ContDiffOn.continuousOn_fderiv_of_isOpen). So v ↦ Dψ(v) and v ↦ D(Φ∘ψ)(v) are continuous on V.
4. (J∘ψ on V.) Let v ∈ V. Φ is differentiable at ψ(v) because it is C¹. Apply the sibling chart_gram_factor with r = 1 to the chart of step 1, Q, Φ and v. It gives det(⟨Dψ(v)e_k, Dψ(v)e_l⟩) > 0, so γ(Dψ(v)) > 0, and γ(D(Φ∘ψ)(v)) = J(ψ(v))·γ(Dψ(v)). Hence J(ψ(v)) = H(v) := γ(D(Φ∘ψ)(v)) / γ(Dψ(v)) for every v ∈ V.
5. (H is continuous on V.) By steps 2–3 the numerator and the denominator of H are continuous on V. By step 4 the denominator does not vanish on V. So H is continuous on V.
6. (Inverse of the chart.) ψ is continuous on V (it is C¹) and injective on V, ψ(V) = W ∩ N ⊆ W, and ψ is proper in the sense of step 1. So the sibling chart_inverse_continuity gives: for every ε' > 0 there is δ' > 0 such that every v' ∈ V with |ψ(v') − ψ(v₀)| < δ' satisfies |v' − v₀| < ε'. This is Simon's remark after (4.1). Indeed, if ψ(v_j) → ψ(v₀) with v_j ∈ V, the v_j lie in the compact set V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K), where K = {ψ(v₀)} ∪ {ψ(v_j)}. Every cluster point v* ∈ V has ψ(v*) = ψ(v₀), hence v* = v₀.
7. (ε–δ.) Let ε > 0. By step 5 there is δ₁ > 0 with |H(v') − H(v₀)| < ε for all v' ∈ V with |v' − v₀| < δ₁. By step 6 with ε' = δ₁ there is δ₂ > 0 such that v' ∈ V and |ψ(v') − y| < δ₂ imply |v' − v₀| < δ₁. Since W is open and y ∈ W, there is δ₃ > 0 with B(y, δ₃) ⊆ W. Put δ := min(δ₂, δ₃) > 0, and let y' ∈ N with |y' − y| < δ. Then y' ∈ W ∩ N = ψ(V), so y' = ψ(v') with v' ∈ V. From |ψ(v') − ψ(v₀)| < δ₂ we get |v' − v₀| < δ₁. By step 4, |J(y') − J(y)| = |H(v') − H(v₀)| < ε.
8. So J is continuous at every y ∈ N relative to N, i.e. J is continuous on N. If N = ∅ this is vacuous. ∎

subproblems.statement: Let P, m, r ∈ ℕ with r ≥ 1. Let N, W ⊆ ℝ^P and V ⊆ ℝ^m, and let ψ : ℝ^m → ℝ^P be a local representation of N as in Simon (4.1). That is: V and W are open; ψ is C^r on V and injective on V; ψ(V) = W ∩ N; V ∩ ψ⁻¹(K) is compact for every compact K ⊆ W; and Dψ(z) is injective for z ∈ V. Let Q : ℝ^P → {linear subspaces of ℝ^P} satisfy Q(x) = T_xN as sets for every x ∈ N. Let Φ : ℝ^P → ℝ^P be C¹ and injective, with DΦ(x) injective for every x. Let J(x) := (det(⟨DΦ(x)τ_i(x), DΦ(x)τ_j(x)⟩)_{i,j<dim Q(x)})^{1/2}, where τ(x) = stdOrthonormalBasis ℝ (Q x). Then for every Borel set B ⊆ W ∩ N and every g : ℝ^P → [0, ∞] (not necessarily measurable), ∫⁻_{Φ(B)} g dH^m = ∫⁻_B ofReal(J(x))·g(Φ(x)) dH^m(x). Here H^m = μHE[m] and ∫⁻ is the lower Lebesgue integral.

Source. Simon Ch. 2, 3.2 and 3.5 (book/chapter-02.txt lines 756–794): the area formula for a 1:1 parametrization and its weighted form. Also 4.11–4.13 (lines 958–994). This child is step 7 of the parent proof, carried out for an arbitrary weight. That covers on each chart the passage to non-negative functions that the parent proof performs globally in step 9. Siblings used: chart_gram_factor (Submission.codim1_ac_saf_chart_gram_factor) and gram_area (Submission.codim1_lura_gram_area_formula).

Weighted parametric area formula (PAF = sibling gram_area, part (ii)). Let f : ℝ^m → ℝ^P and let s ⊆ ℝ^m be Borel. Assume f is differentiable at every x ∈ s, Df(x) is injective for x ∈ s, and f is injective on s. Then for every g : ℝ^P → [0, ∞], measurable or not,
 ∫⁻_{f(s)} g dH^m = ∫⁻_s ofReal(J_f(x))·g(f(x)) dλ(x),
where J_f(x) := √det(⟨Df(x)e_k, Df(x)e_l⟩)_{k,l<m}, e_k = EuclideanSpace.single k 1, H^m = μHE[m] on ℝ^P, and λ is Lebesgue measure (volume) on ℝ^m.
- This is Simon 3.2/3.5.
- The set version H^m(f(A')) = ∫_{A'} J_f dλ for Borel A' ⊆ s says that H^m⌞f(s) is the image of J_f·λ⌞s under the Borel isomorphism f|_s (Lusin–Souslin). Integrating an arbitrary weight against that image measure is exactly the argument of parent steps 7 and 9.

Proof. Fix a Borel set B ⊆ W ∩ N and g : ℝ^P → [0, ∞].
1. (Parameter set.) Let A := V ∩ ψ⁻¹(B).
- A is Borel. ψ is continuous on the open, hence Borel, set V. So the function equal to ψ on V and to 0 off V is Borel measurable (ContinuousOn.measurable_piecewise). And A = V ∩ (this function)⁻¹(B).
- ψ(A) = B. Clearly ψ(A) ⊆ B. Conversely, if b ∈ B ⊆ W ∩ N = ψ(V), then b = ψ(v) with v ∈ V, and v ∈ A.
2. (Hypotheses of PAF.) Let v ∈ A ⊆ V.
- ψ is C^r with r ≥ 1 on the open set V, so it is differentiable at v, and Dψ(v) is injective.
- Φ is C¹, hence differentiable everywhere. So Φ∘ψ is differentiable at v with D(Φ∘ψ)(v) = DΦ(ψ(v))∘Dψ(v) (chain rule). This is injective as a composition of injective maps.
- ψ is injective on A ⊆ V. Φ∘ψ is injective on A because Φ is injective and ψ is injective on V.
3. (PAF for f = Φ∘ψ, s = A, weight g.) Since (Φ∘ψ)(A) = Φ(ψ(A)) = Φ(B):
 ∫⁻_{Φ(B)} g dH^m = ∫⁻_A ofReal(J_{Φ∘ψ}(v))·g(Φ(ψ(v))) dλ(v).
4. (PAF for f = ψ, s = A, weight h(x) := ofReal(J(x))·g(Φ(x)).) Since ψ(A) = B:
 ∫⁻_B ofReal(J(x))·g(Φ(x)) dH^m(x) = ∫⁻_A ofReal(J_ψ(v))·(ofReal(J(ψ(v)))·g(Φ(ψ(v)))) dλ(v).
5. (The integrands agree on A.) Let v ∈ A.
- Apply the sibling chart_gram_factor (same r and chart, Q, Φ differentiable at ψ(v), v ∈ V). Its second conclusion reads, in the notation above, J_{Φ∘ψ}(v) = J(ψ(v))·J_ψ(v).
- J(ψ(v)) ≥ 0 because it is a square root, so ofReal(J_{Φ∘ψ}(v)) = ofReal(J(ψ(v)))·ofReal(J_ψ(v)) (ENNReal.ofReal_mul).
- By commutativity and associativity in [0, ∞], the integrand of step 3 equals the integrand of step 4 at v.
6. (Conclusion.) A is Borel and the two integrands agree on A, so their set integrals over A coincide (setLIntegral_congr_fun). By steps 3 and 4, ∫⁻_{Φ(B)} g dH^m = ∫⁻_B ofReal(J(x))·g(Φ(x)) dH^m(x). Both auxiliary integrals are over A with respect to λ, so H^m on ℝ^m never needs to be compared with λ. ∎
